recent_posts.title: PGKeeper: Building the bouncer we needed for Postgres
recent_posts.summary: Figma outgrew PgBouncer due to its single-threaded architecture, lack of load management, and limited extensibility. They built PGKeeper, a Go-based gRPC service that replaces PgBouncer as the connection pooler in front of their Postgres fleet. PGKeeper introduces pool warming, token-bucket rate limiting for connection creation and teardown, connection churn avoidance (bounded exhaust, auto rollback, context cancellation handling), and a two-stage admission control system. The first stage uses a priority-based semaphore with CoDel and adaptive LIFO scheduling; the second uses a weighted min-max fair sharing tree across multiple traffic dimensions. Rollout used incremental deployment ordered by criticality, load testing at 3× peak QPS, and an automatic error detector that could flip traffic back to PgBouncer. Since full rollout, Figma's database SLO has held above 99.99%, with PGKeeper preventing over 20 user-visible incidents in Q4 2025 alone.

recent_posts.title: Workflow lab: Expanding the canvas with Figma MCP
recent_posts.summary: Figma's MCP server enables a new workflow where AI agents bridge the gap between design and code. Using tools like use_figma and generate_figma_design, agents can read a coded product, generate editable Figma frames for every state (including edge cases like error and loading states), detect design token drift between Figma and the codebase, and document visual differences as shared artifacts. The result is a continuous loop where the canvas reflects the full product reality, designers can iterate freely before committing to code, and handoff happens through Dev Mode without extra review cycles.

recent_posts.title: How to design agentic tools for work
recent_posts.summary: The Google Cloud AI design team behind Gemini Enterprise shares their UX philosophy for building agentic, multi-agent workflows in a business context. Key design decisions include an AI Inbox dashboard for monitoring agent activity, shared persistent project spaces for team collaboration, transparent 'thinking state' narration with source citations, and a governance layer (Agent Designer) that lets users define what data and tools agents can access. The team emphasizes that trust, clarity, and user control are foundational — users should focus on their goals, not on managing AI. Figma and FigJam serve as the design system backbone throughout the process.

recent_posts.title: FigJam is now your coding agent’s whiteboard too
recent_posts.summary: Figma has launched new MCP skills and tools that integrate FigJam with AI coding agents. The new `figma-use-figjam` MCP skill lets agents read and write directly to FigJam boards, while `generate-project-plan` converts docs, codebases, and conversations into visual boards. The workflow enables engineers to turn agent-generated plans into interactive architecture and ER diagrams for team review before implementation. The `get_figjam` tool then brings board content back into the coding environment. Currently in free beta, the integration works with MCP clients including Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, Copilot, and Augment.

recent_posts.title: How AI leaders are borrowing from the design playbook
recent_posts.summary: AI leaders are increasingly adopting design principles to guide organizational AI transformation. Five key principles are outlined: hands-on use of AI tools to build fluency, observing how teams actually use AI to identify friction points, prototyping ideas to make them tangible and shareable, building critique processes to refine AI workflows, and investing in community for continuous shared learning. The argument is that effective AI leadership requires thinking like a designer, not just a technologist.

recent_posts.title: The TL;DR on MCP: Why context matters and how to put it to work
recent_posts.summary: Figma's MCP server connects design files to AI coding tools by exposing structured context — components, tokens, layout decisions — rather than just visual screenshots. This enables AI agents to generate code that references actual design system components and tokens, reducing manual translation between design and code. The post explains how MCP benefits designers (files carry more weight, mistakes travel further), developers (less guesswork, more accurate code generation), and whole teams (roundtrip design loop between canvas and code). Practical setup advice covers using Skills (markdown files guiding agent behavior), investing in a well-structured design system with named layers, auto layout, real components, and code syntax on variables, plus connecting codebases via Code Connect.

recent_posts.title: Turning prompts into five scalable workflows with Figma Weave
recent_posts.summary: Figma Weave (formerly Weavy) is an AI-native creative workflow canvas that chains prompts and AI nodes together for scalable media production. Five practical workflows are demonstrated using a fictional brand called Epoch: (1) combining two reference images to define a reusable style guide using Image Describer nodes, (2) generating on-brand variations across multiple aspect ratios, (3) applying and comparing multiple distortion effects simultaneously, (4) converting images into rotatable 3D models using Rodin 3D V2, and (5) compositing static assets into a final video rendering. The result is a full brand asset system—images, videos, and 3D models—produced from just two reference images without a photoshoot. Figma plans a deeper integration between Weave and Figma Design later in 2026.

recent_posts.title: How Figma used its own AI tools to build mini games in days
recent_posts.summary: Figma's internal team used Figma Make, Figma Weave, and the Figma MCP server to build six mini games (the FigCade) for their annual April Fun Day hackathon. The project showcased how AI tools accelerated prototyping, visual asset creation, and design-to-code workflows. Engineers used Claude and GitHub Copilot authenticated via the Figma MCP server to generate code matching design specs. The team highlighted tighter feedback loops, cross-functional collaboration, and the ability to work outside traditional swimlanes as key benefits of AI-assisted workflows.

recent_posts.title: Build with more context and more control in Figma Make
recent_posts.summary: Figma has launched two new features for Figma Make: Make kits and Make attachments. Make kits allow design system authors to package their components, styles, and usage guidelines (via npm packages or Figma libraries) so AI-generated prototypes start from production-aligned components rather than generic ones. Make attachments let users supply real project context—PDFs, CSVs, JSON datasets, screenshots, brand guidelines, and more—directly into the prompt, so prototypes reflect actual data, edge cases, and constraints instead of idealized placeholders. Together, these features reduce the gap between AI-generated drafts and shippable designs, speeding up review cycles and improving collaboration between designers and engineers. The post also mentions the Figma MCP server, which connects design and code workflows.

recent_posts.title: Agents, meet the Figma canvas
recent_posts.summary: Figma has opened its canvas to AI agents via a new MCP server, allowing tools like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor to read and write directly to Figma files using your existing design system components and variables. A new 'skills' system lets teams encode their design conventions as markdown files, guiding agents to produce brand-aligned, consistent outputs. Nine example skills are available at launch, covering tasks like generating components from codebases, syncing design tokens, applying spacing systems, and running parallel multi-agent workflows. The feature is currently free in beta and works with MCP clients including Augment, Copilot in VS Code, Cursor, and Warp, with plans to expand functionality toward Plugin API parity.
